# C202 Chapter 12 Study Guide: Creating a Healthy Work Environment

*A 15-20 minute read, organized by the chapter's sections in order. Read it before drilling the deck. Each concept covers what it is, why it matters, an example, and how it connects to the rest of the chapter. Worked calculations are included where the text has numbers worth practicing.*

## How this chapter maps to your competencies

This chapter belongs to **Effective Human Resource Management**: *evaluating HRM strategies, policies, and procedures*. Effective HRM is about **52%** of the Objective Assessment (OA), covering Chapters 4-8, 12, and 13. OSHA, HIPAA wellness rules, and drug-free workplace law also touch **Legal and Regulatory** material, so those cards are tagged Legal.

WGU's checklist for this chapter:

1. Explain the concept “culture of safety.”
2. Explain the primary goal of OSHA.
3. Describe how employee wellness programs benefit employers and employees.
4. Explain the difference between functional and dysfunctional stress.
5. Identify forms of bullying at work.
6. Recommend ways to protect employees and others from workplace violence.
7. Describe how providing a safe workplace impacts employee engagement and motivation

The guide follows Antonio through CloudNine's "Project Vitality" launch. It asks you to explain a culture of safety in two or three sentences and OSHA's primary goal in one or two; to label wellness outcomes as benefiting the Employee, the Employer, or Both; to label each day of a stressful week as functional or dysfunctional stress; to pick out bullying behaviors; to recommend three workplace violence protections; and to fill in a word bank (engaged, trust, motivation, retention) about how safety affects engagement. The deck's Apply cards test each of these with new examples.

Chapter 12 closes **Quarter 3** (Chapters 9-12). WGU's strongest readiness signal for the Pre-Assessment is scoring **80% or higher** on the final e-text quiz.

---

## 12.1-12.3 Why a healthy workplace matters

Safety is an **investment, not an expense**: safer workplaces are more efficient and economical. Risks are everywhere, from slips, trips, and falls to repetitive motion injuries among computer users and grocery checkers. Healthier employees are more productive, take fewer sick and disability days, and cost less. **Employee wellness programs** make healthy behavior the norm, and some firms get $6 or more back for every $1 spent. A healthy environment influences both what employees **can** do and what they **will** do.

*Opening case:* Johnson & Johnson was among the first companies with on-site health centers and health risk assessments, and it set out to build the world's healthiest workforce by making healthy choices easy.

*Worked ROI example (from the text):* IBM spent $79 million on wellness over four years and saved about $191 million. Net savings = $191M − $79M = **$112M**, and the return is $191M ÷ $79M ≈ **$2.42 saved per $1 spent**.

## 12.4 Employee safety

U.S. workplace deaths have fallen to about 5,000 a year, but millions of nonfatal injuries still occur. (The book says the ~14,000-deaths figure was from "forty years ago"; it actually dates to 1970, so don't memorize the comparison.) Injuries cost a large share of GDP, raise workers' comp and insurance costs, and hurt productivity, morale, and retention. The top cause of disabling injuries is **overexertion from lifting, pulling, pushing, holding, carrying, or throwing**, followed by falls and being struck by objects.

BP's Deepwater Horizon disaster grew out of failures in equipment, risk management, site culture, and maintenance, after leaders put shareholder value ahead of safety. ExxonMobil treats safety as a leading indicator of organizational quality. HR's role is to hire and train the right people and to build a safety culture through hiring, training, appraisal, incentives, and separations; HR should be the company's **conscience on safety**. In one company, accidents rose 105% when overtime topped 12.5 hours a week for three weeks, and hiring more staff saved $370 million in six months.

## 12.5 A culture of safety (checklist item 1)

A **safety culture** is the shared safety attitudes, beliefs, and practices that shape safety behavior. In a strong safety culture, **everyone is responsible for safety every day** and is willing to flag and fix unsafe behaviors and conditions, not just the safety department.

*Two-to-three-sentence answer (guide style):* A culture of safety is a workplace where shared attitudes, beliefs, and practices make safety everyone's daily responsibility. Employees and managers speak up about hazards, fix unsafe conditions, and treat safety as a core value rather than a rule imposed from outside.

What shapes it: management and employee attitudes; supervisor priorities and accountability; management and employee **norms, beliefs, and assumptions**; safety training and motivation; involvement and commitment; production and financial pressures; and whether unsafe acts actually get corrected. The **most important factor is the CEO making safety a core value**; otherwise production and profit win. Leaders can show the direct and indirect costs of accidents, train everyone in hazard recognition, and celebrate safe behavior. Poor safety culture was blamed for both Deepwater Horizon and Fukushima.

**Reduce hazards; don't punish injuries.** A **safety risk assessment** examines the workplace to identify hazards, evaluate each risk, and decide how to eliminate or control it. Disciplining people for having accidents encourages hiding them: the text reports **2.48 unreported accidents for every reported one**. Disciplining only after an injury is an "anti-injury-reporting program," not a safety program. Safety incentives can build buzz, but OSHA warns that incentives big enough to discourage reporting violate its recordkeeping rules. At Alcoa, Paul O'Neill required a prevention plan for every injury; engagement, quality, and productivity rose, and profits quintupled.

*Worked example:* if a plant records 20 accidents and the 2.48 ratio holds, about 20 × 2.48 ≈ **50 more go unreported**, roughly 70 in total. That's why reporting matters more than a low recorded count.

## 12.6 Ergonomics

**Ergonomics** is designing the work environment (lighting, furniture, layout, lifting, vibration, temperature) to reduce physical and psychological demands, so performance improves and injuries and errors fall. **Cumulative trauma disorders** are muscle and skeletal injuries from repeatedly using the same muscles; **carpal tunnel syndrome** is a common hand and wrist example among typists, chefs, and assembly workers. Prevention includes training on risk factors, redesigning tools and workstations, adjustable workstations, work-rest schedules, regular breaks, and task rotation. (The text calls repetitive-motion injuries the most common hazard in one place and lifting injuries the top cause of disabling injury in another; they're different measures, so the deck doesn't test which is "most common.")

## 12.7-12.8 OSHA (checklist item 2)

The **Occupational Safety and Health Act (1970)** requires every employer with at least one employee to provide a workplace **free from recognized hazards likely to cause death or serious harm**. It created **OSHA**, which sets and enforces standards and provides information, training, and assistance.

*One-to-two-sentence answer (guide style):* OSHA's primary goal is to prevent work-related injuries, illnesses, and deaths by setting and enforcing safety standards and helping employers correct hazards. It supports employees through inspections, training, and protection from retaliation when they raise concerns. The text stresses that OSHA's goal is **correcting hazards and compliance, not collecting fines**.

**Employer duties:** follow standards; find and correct hazards; communicate chemical hazards (labels, training, safety data sheets); provide required protective equipment at no cost; keep injury and illness records; post citations, injury summaries, and the "It's the Law" poster; and never retaliate. **Reporting (current rule):** report a **fatality within 8 hours** and **any single inpatient hospitalization, amputation, or eye loss within 24 hours**. *Erratum:* the book's "three or more workers hospitalized" trigger is the pre-2015 rule; the OSHA poster on the same page shows the current one.

**Worker rights:** a safe workplace; training in understandable language; access to injury records, hazard test results, and their medical records; requesting a confidential inspection; talking privately with the inspector; and filing a retaliation complaint **within 30 days**.

**OSHA Form 300** logs work-related injuries and illnesses. A case must be recorded **within 7 calendar days** if it involves death, loss of consciousness, restricted work or transfer, medical treatment beyond first aid, or certain diagnosed conditions.

**Standards** are legally required protections (fall protection, machine guards, respirators, blood-borne pathogens). The **General Duty Clause** covers serious recognized hazards when no specific standard applies. The **Hazard Communication Standard** requires labels, safety data sheets, and training for chemical hazards.

**Inspections** come without advance notice, in priority order: imminent danger, fatalities and catastrophes, worker complaints, referrals, follow-ups, then planned inspections of high-hazard industries. Employers can contest any part of a citation; workers can challenge only the abatement deadline; appeals go to the independent Occupational Safety and Health Review Commission. Inspections cut injury rates without hurting sales or jobs. OSHA also offers **free, penalty-free consultations** for small businesses and training through its OTI Education Centers. OSHA doesn't hand out protective equipment itself; employers must provide it.

## 12.9-12.10 Employee wellness (checklist item 3)

**Employee wellness programs** are initiatives that raise company and employee performance or morale through better health. Common focus areas are healthy eating, smoking cessation, weight management, physical activity, and stress management. A **health assessment questionnaire** is the usual starting point; it prompts reflection and lets the program be tailored. The biggest barrier is lack of time during the workday, so the program needs a supportive wellness culture.

**Benefits to the employer:** fewer injuries, lower healthcare costs, less absenteeism, better morale and loyalty, higher productivity, and lower workers' comp and disability costs. **Benefits to employees:** better long-term physical health and energy, less stress, better mental health, and often lower premiums.

*Guide-style sort (who benefits most):* reduced stress and better mental health = **Employee**; lower healthcare costs and insurance premiums = mainly the **Employer** (employees share premiums, so "Both" is defensible); higher engagement and morale = **Both**; fewer sick days = mainly the **Employer**; better long-term health and energy = **Employee**.

Small organizations can still act: lunchtime walks, healthy snacks, local gym discounts, friendly competitions, and limits on after-hours e-mail. Google's simple nudge, putting water at eye level and soda lower, raised water consumption 47%.

**Wellness incentives (12.10).** Rewards raise participation. **Present bias** means people overweight immediate costs and benefits: unhealthy habits feel good now and cost later, while healthy ones cost effort now and pay off later. So small, frequent, tangible rewards (per gym visit) work better than a year-end rebate. The best programs build habits that last after the incentives end. **Perceived fairness** matters: when one company paid smokers to quit, nonsmokers objected, so it switched to a smoker surcharge. State off-duty conduct laws, like New York's smokers' rights law, may limit what employers can do.

**HIPAA rules:** participation-based incentives (such as completing a health assessment) are unlimited if they're available to everyone. Health-contingent incentives (such as reaching a cholesterol target) are capped. *Erratum:* the book says the cap is 20% of total premium; since 2014, under the ACA, the cap is **30% of the total premium cost (50% for tobacco programs)**.

*Worked cap example (hypothetical):* if total annual premium cost is $8,000, the maximum health-contingent reward is 30% × $8,000 = **$2,400**, or up to 50% × $8,000 = **$4,000** for a tobacco-cessation program.

## 12.11 Stress (checklist item 4)

Mild stress helps, because adrenaline aids action and memory. **Functional stress** is manageable stress that produces **positive emotions** like satisfaction, excitement, and enjoyment, such as a challenging new project. **Dysfunctional stress** is under- or over-arousal from **too few or too many demands for too long**, like conflicting goals, a harsh boss, or boredom from too little work. Both can cause emotional exhaustion, but dysfunctional stress is also linked to **withdrawal and turnover**. A lack of stress isn't always good, and prolonged stress of any kind can cause health problems like high blood pressure.

*Guide-style week:* Monday (tight deadlines, clear role, energized) = functional. Tuesday (pressure keeps him focused, timely feedback) = functional. Wednesday (last-minute changes, late nights, skipped breaks, drained) = dysfunctional. Thursday (headache, worry, staring at the screen without progress) = dysfunctional. Friday (relaxed pace, creative spark returning) = functional.

Common triggers are heavy workload, unclear responsibilities, low meaningfulness, long hours, poor work-life balance, and job insecurity. The most important HR remedy is giving employees **more control over their work patterns and schedules**, plus a positive culture, open communication, and **participation in decisions**. **Problem-focused coping** (addressing the cause) is more effective than **emotion-focused coping** (managing feelings). Regular exercise, social support, and rest help; drinking and overeating hurt. Financial stress is a top stressor, and financial wellness programs can return more than 300%.

## 12.12-12.13 Bullying and substance abuse (checklist item 5)

**Workplace bullying** is a repeated pattern of behavior intended to intimidate, offend, degrade, or humiliate a person or group. Forms include **verbal abuse; public criticism and humiliation; sarcasm and dismissing ideas; threats and intimidation; excluding or ignoring someone; unreasonable or menial assignments; teasing and gossip; different performance standards; and work interference or sabotage**. Targets suffer anxiety, depression, and lower satisfaction, and about 20% quit; employers pay through workers' comp, disability, and reputation. Most bullies are managers.

*Guide-style pick:* repeated public criticism, sarcastic dismissal of ideas, excluding someone from key emails and meetings, and raising one's voice to humiliate are **bullying**. Specific constructive feedback in private and clear expectations about deadlines are **not**.

Prevention: a supportive culture; a zero-tolerance policy that defines bullying and explains reporting and investigation; training for new managers; repeated communication that empowers bystanders; structured interviews to screen; and firing bullies. Cisco runs a global civility program.

**Substance abuse:** a **drug-free workplace** has policies ensuring employees aren't using, selling, or impaired by alcohol or illegal drugs. The **Drug-Free Workplace Act of 1988** requires some federal contractors and all federal grantees to provide one. A comprehensive program has five parts: a written policy, supervisor training, employee education, an **employee assistance program (EAP)** offering confidential counseling, and drug testing. OSHA doesn't require these programs, and state testing laws vary.

## 12.15 Sustainable performance and burnout

A **sustainable organization** endures and stays creative and efficient over time by balancing the triple bottom line of people, planet, and profit. Toxic practices like long hours, low control, and unfair treatment harm health without improving performance. **Burnout** is emotional, mental, and physical exhaustion from chronic workplace stress that hasn't been successfully managed. *Erratum:* the book says WHO calls burnout a "workplace hazard"; WHO's 2019 classification calls it an **"occupational phenomenon,"** not a medical condition. **Recovery** (off-job relaxation and detachment) restores energy. **Thriving** is a state of vitality and learning, supported by healthy eating, exercise, sleep, breaks, autonomy, and civility. **Job crafting** means reshaping work to make it more meaningful.

## 12.16 Security and workplace violence (checklist item 6)

**Workplace violence** is any act or threat of physical violence, harassment, intimidation, or threatening disruptive behavior at work, affecting employees, clients, customers, or visitors. Risk factors include handling money with the public, working alone or late at night, serving alcohol, providing care, and high-crime areas. Most incidents stem from **unresolved conflict or domestic issues and loss of control**.

**Recommended protections:**

- A **zero-tolerance policy** covering threats and harassment by anyone (employees, clients, visitors, contractors)
- **Physical security:** keycards, layouts that expose unescorted visitors, silent alarms, and CCTV
- **Training** for managers on early warning signs and for supervisors on avoiding negligent hiring and retention
- **Screening**, including making sure temp agencies screen workers
- **EAPs** and anonymous channels for venting concerns
- Regular **security audits**, risk assessments, and a reviewed emergency plan
- Prompt investigation and discipline, since failing to act encourages more violence

The General Duty Clause can require action when an employee threatens others. Disaster preparedness means a written plan for people, physical resources, and business continuity, practiced with drills.

## 12.17-12.18 J&J's response and safety games

J&J built its program on healthy eating, healthy movement, and a healthy mind, with mental health counseling, financial coaching, apps, and an energy course. Its healthcare costs run 2-3% below most major corporations. Safety games work best when they reward **proactive behaviors** like reporting near misses, suggesting improvements, and attending training, not just the absence of injuries.

## How a safe workplace drives engagement and motivation (checklist item 7)

When employees feel safe, they're more likely to be **engaged** in their roles. A safe environment builds **trust**, so people share ideas, raise concerns, and collaborate without fear. As a result, employees feel more **motivation** to perform, and over time safety improves **retention**, because people stay where they feel protected and supported. Safety also cuts absences, injuries, and costs, freeing energy for the work itself.

## What to be able to explain

These are WGU's Learning Checklist items for this chapter:

1. Explain the concept “culture of safety.”
2. Explain the primary goal of OSHA.
3. Describe how employee wellness programs benefit employers and employees.
4. Explain the difference between functional and dysfunctional stress.
5. Identify forms of bullying at work.
6. Recommend ways to protect employees and others from workplace violence.
7. Describe how providing a safe workplace impacts employee engagement and motivation

To get there, make sure you can also explain:

- Why disciplining injuries backfires, and the 2.48 unreported-accident ratio
- OSHA's 8-hour and 24-hour reporting rules, the 7-day Form 300 rule, and the inspection priorities
- The HIPAA/ACA wellness incentive cap (30%, or 50% for tobacco) and present bias
- Burnout as WHO's "occupational phenomenon," recovery, and thriving

cards.front: How do HIPAA rules treat participation-based vs health-contingent incentives?
cards.answer: Participation-based are unlimited if open to all; health-contingent rewards are capped.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.10 · Legal & Regulatory
points: Participation: completing an assessment; contingent: hitting a target

cards.front: What is the cap on health-contingent wellness incentives?
cards.answer: 30% of total premium cost, or 50% for tobacco programs (ACA, since 2014).
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.10 · Legal & Regulatory
points: Erratum: the book says 20%

cards.front: How do you calculate the maximum health-contingent wellness reward?
cards.answer: Total premium × 30% (50% for tobacco). An $8,000 premium allows $2,400, or $4,000 for tobacco.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.10 · Legal & Regulatory
points: Hypothetical premium

cards.front: What do state off-duty conduct laws mean for wellness programs?
cards.answer: Some states protect lawful off-hours activity, such as smoking, limiting employer penalties.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.10 · Legal & Regulatory
points: New York 'smokers' rights'; California broader

cards.front: What is functional stress?
cards.answer: Manageable stress that produces positive emotions like satisfaction, excitement, and enjoyment.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.11 · Effective HRM
points: Example: a challenging new project

cards.front: What is dysfunctional stress?
cards.answer: Under- or over-arousal from too few or too many demands for too long.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.11 · Effective HRM
points: Conflicting goals, harsh boss, boredom

cards.front: How do the outcomes of functional and dysfunctional stress differ?
cards.answer: Both can cause exhaustion, but only dysfunctional stress is also linked to withdrawal and turnover.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.11 · Effective HRM
points: Functional stress can raise satisfaction

cards.front: Is a total lack of stress always good?
cards.answer: No. Mild stress aids action and memory, and too few demands (boredom) is itself dysfunctional.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.11 · Effective HRM
points: Prolonged stress of any kind can harm health

cards.front: What are common workplace stress triggers?
cards.answer: Heavy workload, unclear responsibilities, low meaningfulness, long hours, poor balance, job insecurity.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.11 · Effective HRM
points: Prolonged stress raises blood pressure and cholesterol

cards.front: What is HR's most important lever for reducing stress?
cards.answer: Giving employees more control over their work patterns and schedules.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.11 · Effective HRM
points: Also positive culture, open communication, participation

cards.front: What is the difference between problem-focused and emotion-focused coping?
cards.answer: Problem-focused tackles the cause (more effective); emotion-focused manages the feelings.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.11 · Effective HRM
points: Removing the source beats managing symptoms

cards.front: What are healthy vs harmful ways to cope with stress?
cards.answer: Healthy: exercise, social support, humor, meditation, rest. Harmful: drinking, drugs, overeating.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.11 · Effective HRM
points: Regular moderate exercise is among the best

cards.front: What manager actions reduce employee stress?
cards.answer: Match workload to capability, clarify roles, design meaningful jobs, allow participation, enable stress breaks.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.11 · Effective HRM
points: Positive feedback and strengths-based work energize

cards.front: What is workplace bullying?
cards.answer: A repeated pattern of behavior meant to intimidate, offend, degrade, or humiliate a person or group.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.12 · Effective HRM
points: About 71% of bullies are managers

cards.front: What forms can workplace bullying take?
cards.answer: Verbal abuse, public humiliation, sarcasm, threats, exclusion, menial assignments, gossip, sabotage.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.12 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 12.12 Bullying; 12.19 Summary and Application
points: Also different performance standards

cards.front: What separates bullying from tough management?
cards.answer: Bullying is repeated, personal, and humiliating; tough management is specific, job-focused, and respectful.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.12 · Effective HRM
points: Private constructive feedback isn't bullying

cards.front: What does bullying cost employers?
cards.answer: Higher workers' comp and disability costs, turnover (about 20% of targets quit), and reputation damage.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.12 · Effective HRM
points: Targets suffer anxiety, depression, PTSD

cards.front: How can organizations prevent bullying?
cards.answer: Zero-tolerance policy with reporting steps, manager training, bystander awareness, screening, firing bullies.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.12 · Effective HRM
points: Cisco's global civility program

cards.front: What is a drug-free workplace?
cards.answer: Policies ensuring employees aren't using, selling, or impaired by alcohol or illegal drugs at work.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.13 · Effective HRM
points: Includes after-effects like hangovers

cards.front: What does the Drug-Free Workplace Act of 1988 require?
cards.answer: Some federal contractors and all federal grantees must maintain a drug-free workplace.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.13 · Legal & Regulatory
points: OSHA doesn't require drug programs

cards.front: What are the five parts of a comprehensive substance abuse program?
cards.answer: Written policy, supervisor training, employee education, an EAP, and drug testing.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.13 · Effective HRM
points: Policy backed by top management, consistently enforced

cards.front: What is an employee assistance program (EAP)?
cards.answer: Confidential counseling for employees and families on many personal problems, in-house or contracted.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.13 · Effective HRM
points: Also used for stress and violence prevention

cards.front: How did J&J's 'Live for Life' incentive work?
cards.answer: A $500 premium discount for a confidential health assessment, kept if healthy or in risk management.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.14 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 12.14 Case Study: Johnson & Johnson's Wellness Programs
points: Savings >$250M in 10 years (~3x return)

cards.front: What is a sustainable organization?
cards.answer: One that endures and stays creative and efficient by balancing people, planet, and profit.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.15 · Effective HRM
points: OSHA: can't be sustainable without protecting workers

cards.front: What is burnout?
cards.answer: Emotional, mental, and physical exhaustion from chronic workplace stress that wasn't successfully managed.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.15 · Effective HRM
points: WHO (2019): an 'occupational phenomenon'; book says 'workplace hazard'

cards.front: What is recovery, in sustainable performance?
cards.answer: Off-job relaxation and psychological detachment that restore next-day energy and engagement.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.15 · Effective HRM
points: Wachovia's energy-renewal program raised revenue

cards.front: What is thriving at work?
cards.answer: A positive state of vitality and learning that raises satisfaction, performance, and health.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.15 · Effective HRM
points: Built on eating, exercise, sleep, breaks, autonomy

cards.front: What is job crafting?
cards.answer: Reshaping one's work to make it more meaningful, such as focusing on helping others.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.15 · Effective HRM
points: Supports thriving

cards.front: What is the Business Roundtable's view of corporate purpose?
cards.answer: Large-company CEOs committing to invest in employees and serve all stakeholders, not just shareholders.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.15 · Effective HRM
points: About 180 CEOs

cards.front: How do leaders who model sustainable work affect employees?
cards.answer: Their employees are more engaged, more satisfied, likelier to stay, and more trusting.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.15 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 12.10 Wellness Incentives; 12.15 Creating Sustainable Performance
points: 55% more engaged; 77% more satisfied

cards.front: What is workplace violence?
cards.answer: Any act or threat of physical violence, harassment, intimidation, or threatening disruption at work.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.16 · Effective HRM
points: Affects employees, clients, customers, visitors

cards.front: What are risk factors for workplace violence?
cards.answer: Handling money, working alone or late, serving alcohol, providing care, unstable people, high-crime areas.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.16 · Effective HRM
points: High risk: delivery, healthcare, law enforcement

cards.front: What causes most workplace violence?
cards.answer: Unresolved conflict or domestic issues and a loss of control.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.16 · Effective HRM
points: EAPs, caring supervisors, venting channels help

cards.front: What should a workplace violence prevention program include?
cards.answer: Zero tolerance, physical security, warning-sign training, screening, EAPs, audits, and a reviewed emergency plan.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.16 · Effective HRM
points: Prompt investigation and discipline

cards.front: Why should a zero-tolerance violence policy cover non-employees?
cards.answer: Threats can come from clients, patients, visitors, and contractors, not just staff.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.16 · Effective HRM
points: Also cover threats and harassment, not only physical acts

cards.front: Why train supervisors on hiring and retention to prevent violence?
cards.answer: To avoid negligent hiring and retention of people with a known risk of violence.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.16 · Effective HRM
points: Also make sure temp agencies screen

cards.front: Why do anonymous venting channels help prevent violence?
cards.answer: They let people air conflicts before they escalate.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.16 · Effective HRM
points: Most violence stems from unresolved conflict

cards.front: What should a disaster preparedness plan cover?
cards.answer: People, physical resources, and business continuity, tested with training and drills.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.16 · Effective HRM
points: Red Cross guidance; off-site data backups

cards.front: What three pillars anchor J&J's health strategy?
cards.answer: Healthy eating, healthy movement, and a healthy mind.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.17 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 12.17 Real World Response: J&J's Quest for the Healthiest Workforce
points: Plus financial well-being coaching

cards.front: What should safety games and incentives reward?
cards.answer: Proactive behaviors: following policies, reporting near misses, suggesting fixes, attending training.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.18 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 12.18 Strategic HRM Exercise: Fun and Games Improve Safety Performance
points: Not just the absence of injuries

cards.front: How does a safe workplace affect engagement and motivation?
cards.answer: Safety builds trust, so people engage, speak up, feel motivated, and stay longer.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.19 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 12.19 Summary and Application; 12.4 Employee Safety
points: Word bank: engaged, trust, motivation, retention

cards.front: Why does feeling safe make employees more likely to speak up?
cards.answer: Trust removes fear of harm or retaliation, so people share ideas and raise concerns.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.19 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 12.19 Summary and Application; 12.5 A Culture of Safety
points: Psychological safety supports engagement

cards.front: Which is the best 2-3 sentence explanation of a culture of safety?
choices: The safety officer owns safety; other employees focus on output and leave all hazard reporting to that one role.
Safety means meeting OSHA's minimum rules; anything beyond the posted standards is a cost the firm should avoid.
Safety is mainly about punishing employees who get hurt, so that others learn to be careful and avoid injuries.
Everyone shares safety values and practices and owns safety daily; hazards get reported and fixed, not hidden.
cards.explanation: The guide's activity: a culture of safety is shared attitudes, beliefs, and practices where everyone is responsible for safety every day.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.5 Apply · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 12.5 A Culture of Safety

cards.front: A plant manager wants to cut reported injuries fast by docking pay for anyone injured. What's the likely result?
choices: A real drop in injuries and hazards
Lower workers' comp cost long term
cards.explanation: Punishing injuries discourages reporting; it becomes an anti-reporting program, and OSHA may treat it as a recordkeeping violation.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.5 Apply · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 12.5 A Culture of Safety

cards.front: A mine has 20 reported accidents this year. Using the text's ratio, about how many went unreported?
cards.explanation: 20 × 2.48 ≈ 49.6, so roughly 50 unreported accidents.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.5 Apply · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 12.5 A Culture of Safety

cards.front: A new CEO wants a real safety culture. What should come first?
choices: Make safety a stated core value
cards.explanation: The single most important factor is the CEO making safety a core value; otherwise production pressures win.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.5 Apply · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 12.5 A Culture of Safety

cards.front: A safety team walks the floor listing hazards, rating each risk, and choosing controls. What is this?
cards.explanation: A safety risk assessment identifies hazards, evaluates risks, and decides how to eliminate or control them.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.5 Apply · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 12.5 A Culture of Safety

cards.front: Two supervisors enforce safety rules very differently. What does the research predict?
cards.explanation: Inconsistent enforcement and a poor safety climate are linked to more unreported accidents.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.5 Apply · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 12.5 A Culture of Safety

cards.front: A firm wants a safety contest that won't suppress reporting. Which design fits best?
choices: Fines for each injury a worker reports
Points for near-miss reports and training
A prize for zero recorded injuries
Team bonuses lost when anyone is hurt
cards.explanation: Reward proactive behaviors, like reporting near misses and attending training, not just the absence of injuries.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.18 Apply · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 12.18 Strategic HRM Exercise: Fun and Games Improve Safety Performance

cards.front: A refinery's leaders praise output records while maintenance is deferred. Which disaster does this echo?
cards.explanation: Deepwater Horizon followed failures in risk management, culture, and maintenance where profit trumped safety.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.4 Apply · Effective HRM

cards.front: Which is the best 1-2 sentence explanation of OSHA's primary goal?
choices: To handle discrimination charges so that hazardous jobs are assigned fairly across protected groups.
To prevent work-related injuries, illnesses, and deaths by setting and enforcing standards and helping employers.
To collect fines from employers; penalties fund the agency and are its main measure of success each year.
To set minimum wages and overtime rules so that every worker is paid fairly for hazardous assignments.
cards.explanation: The guide's activity: OSHA's goal is to ensure safe, healthful working conditions and prevent injuries, illnesses, and deaths.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.7 Apply · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 12.7 The Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA)

cards.front: A worker dies on the job at 6 a.m. By when must the employer report it to OSHA?
cards.explanation: Fatalities must be reported within 8 hours. (Hospitalization, amputation, or eye loss: 24 hours.)
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.7 Apply · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 12.7 The Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA)

cards.front: One employee is admitted to the hospital overnight after a fall. What must the employer do?
choices: Report it to OSHA within 24 hours
Report nothing; it's a single case
Report only if 3 or more are admitted
cards.explanation: Since 2015, any single inpatient hospitalization must be reported within 24 hours. The book's '3+ hospitalized' trigger is outdated.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.7 Apply · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 12.7 The Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA)

cards.front: An employee needs stitches (beyond first aid) after a cut. By when must it go on the OSHA 300 log?
cards.explanation: Recordable cases (beyond-first-aid treatment, restricted work, etc.) go on Form 300 within 7 calendar days.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.7 Apply · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 12.7 The Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA)

cards.front: A welder is demoted a week after reporting a hazard. What can she do, and by when?
choices: Request arbitration within a full year
File a retaliation complaint within 30 days
Nothing; OSHA covers only physical injuries
Sue under Title VII within 7 days of it
cards.explanation: OSHA bars retaliation; workers have 30 days to file a complaint.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.7 Apply · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 12.7 The Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA)

cards.front: A worker's job requires a respirator. Who pays for it?
choices: The employer, at no cost to the worker
The worker, deducted from each paycheck
OSHA, through a federal safety grant
Split evenly by worker and firm
cards.explanation: Employers must provide required personal protective equipment free of charge.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.7 Apply · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 12.7 The Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA)

cards.front: OSHA has a fatality report, a worker complaint, and a scheduled visit. Which comes first?
cards.explanation: Priorities: imminent danger, fatalities/catastrophes, complaints, referrals, follow-ups, planned inspections.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.8 Apply · Legal & Regulatory

cards.front: A union disagrees with an OSHA citation. What can workers challenge?
cards.explanation: Employers can contest any part; workers can challenge only the time allowed to fix the hazard.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.8 Apply · Legal & Regulatory

cards.front: A warehouse faces a hazard no OSHA standard specifically covers. What applies?
cards.explanation: The General Duty Clause requires workplaces free of serious recognized hazards when no standard applies.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.8 Apply · Legal & Regulatory

cards.front: Workers handle solvents but have no labels or safety data sheets. Which rule is broken?
cards.explanation: The Hazard Communication Standard requires labels, safety data sheets, and training on chemical hazards.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.8 Apply · Legal & Regulatory

cards.front: A 40-person bakery wants OSHA help without risking fines. What should it request?
cards.explanation: OSHA's small-business consultation is free and confidential, with no penalties.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.8 Apply · Legal & Regulatory

cards.front: An owner fears an OSHA inspection will hurt sales. What does the research show?
choices: Firms often close within the next year
Injuries and costs fall; sales don't
cards.explanation: Inspections cut injuries 9.4% and injury costs 26% with no loss in sales, employment, or survival.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.8 Apply · Legal & Regulatory

cards.front: Plant overtime has run 13 hours a week for a month. What should HR expect and do?
cards.explanation: Overtime above 12.5 hours a week for three weeks raised accidents 105%; hiring more staff saved $370M.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.4 Apply · Effective HRM

cards.front: Data-entry clerks report wrist pain from hours of typing. What best fits?
choices: Remove all rest breaks to finish
cards.explanation: Carpal tunnel is a cumulative trauma disorder; ergonomic redesign, training, and work-rest schedules prevent it.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.6 Apply · Effective HRM

cards.front: Assemblers repeat the same motion all shift. Which ergonomic design helps most?
choices: A single fixed posture all shift
Higher piece rates for the same task
cards.explanation: Repetitive work should allow posture changes, regular breaks, and task rotation.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.6 Apply · Effective HRM

cards.front: Wellness outcome sort: reduced stress and better mental health benefit whom most?
cards.explanation: Guide-style sort: reduced stress and better mental health benefit the employee most (moderate confidence on the key).
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.9 Apply · Effective HRM

cards.front: Wellness outcome sort: lower healthcare costs and insurance premiums benefit whom most?
cards.explanation: Guide-style sort: mainly the employer, which funds most of the premium; employees share premiums, so 'Both' is defensible (moderate confidence).
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.9 Apply · Effective HRM

cards.front: Wellness outcome sort: higher engagement and morale benefit whom?
cards.explanation: Guide-style sort: engagement and morale help employees feel better and employers perform better.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.9 Apply · Effective HRM

cards.front: Wellness outcome sort: fewer sick days and absences benefit whom most?
cards.explanation: Guide-style sort: lower absenteeism mainly benefits the employer through productivity (moderate confidence).
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.9 Apply · Effective HRM

cards.front: Wellness outcome sort: better long-term physical health and energy benefit whom most?
cards.explanation: Guide-style sort: long-term health and energy benefit the employee most (moderate confidence).
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.9 Apply · Effective HRM

cards.front: A 25-person firm has no budget for a gym. Which wellness approach fits?
choices: Skip wellness; it needs a large firm
cards.explanation: Small organizations can use local gym discounts, healthy snacks, lunchtime fitness, and friendly competitions.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.9 Apply · Effective HRM

cards.front: Employees like the new wellness program but say they never have time for it. What's the fix?
choices: Add more online content for them to read
cards.explanation: Lack of time during the workday is the biggest barrier; manager and coworker support makes participation possible.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.9 Apply · Effective HRM

cards.front: A cafeteria moves water to eye level and soda to lower shelves. What's this an example of?
cards.explanation: Google's simple placement change raised water consumption 47%: a nudge, not a mandate.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.9 Apply · Effective HRM

cards.front: A wellness program cost $2M and saved $5M. What's the return per dollar?
cards.explanation: $5M ÷ $2M = $2.50 per $1 (net savings $3M). Compare IBM: $191M ÷ $79M ≈ $2.42.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.2 Apply · Effective HRM

cards.front: Which wellness reward is most likely to change behavior, given present bias?
choices: A plaque at the annual dinner
cards.explanation: Present bias favors small, tangible, frequent rewards over distant ones.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.10 Apply · Effective HRM

cards.front: A firm offers $100 to anyone who completes a health assessment. Is it capped under HIPAA?
choices: Yes; capped at 30% of total premium
No; but only smokers may legally receive the reward
No; open-to-all participation rewards aren't capped
cards.explanation: Participation-based incentives aren't capped if available to everyone; health-contingent ones are.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.10 Apply · Legal & Regulatory

cards.front: Total annual premium is $10,000. What's the largest reward for hitting a cholesterol target?
cards.explanation: Health-contingent cap: 30% × $10,000 = $3,000 (the book's 20% is outdated). Tobacco programs: up to 50%.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.10 Apply · Legal & Regulatory

cards.front: Total annual premium is $10,000. What's the largest reward for a tobacco-cessation program?
cards.explanation: ACA: tobacco programs may reach 50% of total premium cost (50% × $10,000 = $5,000).
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.10 Apply · Legal & Regulatory

cards.front: Nonsmokers complain a quit-smoking bonus rewards bad habits. What issue is this?
cards.explanation: Perceived fairness: one firm switched from a smoker reward to a smoker surcharge after such complaints.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.10 Apply · Effective HRM

cards.front: Antonio, Monday: tight deadlines, but a clear role and good tools; he feels energized. Which stress?
cards.explanation: Guide activity: manageable pressure with positive emotions is functional stress.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.11 Apply · Effective HRM

cards.front: Antonio, Tuesday: client pressure keeps him focused, and his manager gives timely feedback. Which stress?
cards.explanation: Guide activity: pressure that sharpens focus with support is functional stress.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.11 Apply · Effective HRM

cards.front: Antonio, Wednesday: last-minute changes, late nights, skipped breaks; he feels drained. Which stress?
cards.explanation: Guide activity: too many demands for too long is dysfunctional stress.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.11 Apply · Effective HRM

cards.front: Antonio, Thursday: a headache and constant worry; he stares at his screen without progress. Which stress?
cards.explanation: Guide activity: physical symptoms and stalled work signal dysfunctional stress.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.11 Apply · Effective HRM

cards.front: Antonio, Friday: a relaxed pace, and his creative spark is returning. Which stress?
cards.explanation: Guide activity: manageable demands and returning energy fit functional stress.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.11 Apply · Effective HRM

cards.front: A clerk has almost nothing to do for months and feels restless and detached. Which stress?
cards.explanation: Too few demands for too long (boredom) is dysfunctional stress; a lack of stress isn't always good.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.11 Apply · Effective HRM

cards.front: Nurses report stress from rigid, unpredictable schedules. What HR change helps most?
cards.explanation: The most important HR remedy is giving employees more control over their work patterns.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.11 Apply · Effective HRM

cards.front: An analyst stressed by vague duties asks his manager to clarify priorities. Which coping style?
cards.explanation: Tackling the cause is problem-focused coping, generally more effective than managing feelings.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.11 Apply · Effective HRM

cards.front: Which manager action best reduces dysfunctional stress on a team?
choices: Add goals that conflict with each other
cards.explanation: Match workload to capability, clarify roles, and allow participation and breaks.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.11 Apply · Effective HRM

cards.front: An employee is exhausted, cynical, and detached after months of unmanaged stress. What is this?
cards.explanation: Burnout is exhaustion from chronic unmanaged workplace stress; WHO (2019) calls it an 'occupational phenomenon.'
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.15 Apply · Effective HRM

cards.front: A manager repeatedly criticizes one employee's work in front of the team. Is it bullying?
choices: No: only physical acts ever count
cards.explanation: Guide activity: repeated public criticism and humiliation is bullying.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.12 Apply · Effective HRM

cards.front: A supervisor meets privately to give specific feedback on how to improve a report. Is it bullying?
choices: Yes: any criticism at all is bullying
cards.explanation: Guide activity: specific, job-focused feedback given privately isn't bullying.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.12 Apply · Effective HRM

cards.front: A coworker meets every idea with sarcasm and dismissive remarks. Is it bullying?
choices: Only if a manager is the one doing it
cards.explanation: Guide activity: repeated sarcasm and dismissing ideas are forms of bullying.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.12 Apply · Effective HRM

cards.front: One employee is regularly left off key emails and meetings needed for her job. Is it bullying?
cards.explanation: Guide activity: excluding or ignoring someone is a form of bullying.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.12 Apply · Effective HRM

cards.front: A manager tells the team clearly when deadlines are and what quality is expected. Is it bullying?
cards.explanation: Guide activity: setting clear expectations is good management, not bullying.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.12 Apply · Effective HRM

cards.front: A supervisor often yells at an employee to humiliate him in front of others. Is it bullying?
choices: No: only HR can judge a manager's tone
cards.explanation: Guide activity: raising one's voice to humiliate is verbal abuse and bullying.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.12 Apply · Effective HRM

cards.front: A manager gives one analyst only menial tasks far below her skills and holds her to tougher standards. Which applies?
cards.explanation: Unreasonable or menial assignments and different performance standards are forms of bullying.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.12 Apply · Effective HRM

cards.front: A firm with frequent bullying complaints wants a first policy step. What fits best?
choices: A zero-tolerance policy with reporting steps
A policy covering physical acts only
Ask targets to toughen up and simply move on
Transfer every target to new teams
cards.explanation: Define bullying, explain reporting and investigation, train managers, and empower bystanders.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.12 Apply · Effective HRM

cards.front: A company holds a federal grant. What must it maintain?
cards.explanation: The Drug-Free Workplace Act of 1988 covers all federal grantees and some federal contractors.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.13 Apply · Legal & Regulatory

cards.front: A firm has a drug policy and testing but nowhere to refer employees for help. Which component is missing?
cards.explanation: The five components are written policy, supervisor training, employee education, an EAP, and drug testing.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.13 Apply · Effective HRM

cards.front: A clinic's policy bans violence only by employees. A patient threatens a nurse. What should change?
choices: Ban only physical assaults by staff
cards.explanation: Zero-tolerance policies should cover threats and harassment by anyone, not just employees.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.16 Apply · Effective HRM

cards.front: A convenience store has one late-night clerk who handles cash. Which protections fit best?
choices: More cash kept on hand in the register at night
No changes; this violence is random
Silent alarms, CCTV, and access control
Longer shifts for that one night clerk
cards.explanation: Handling money and working alone late are risk factors; physical security reduces risk.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.16 Apply · Effective HRM

cards.front: Which set is the best three-part recommendation to protect people from workplace violence?
choices: Ban all visitors, end all training, and arm every staffer
Zero tolerance, warning-sign training, physical security
Bigger bonuses, longer shifts, and fewer breaks
Drop background checks, close the EAP, cut audits
cards.explanation: Guide activity: recommend protections like a zero-tolerance policy, training on warning signs, and physical security, with reasons.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.16 Apply · Effective HRM

cards.front: A temp agency sends workers without background checks. What should HR do?
choices: Require the agency to screen workers
Accept them; it's the agency's risk
Hire only temps to cut liability
Skip screening to fill jobs faster
cards.explanation: Make sure temp agencies screen workers, as part of avoiding negligent hiring.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.16 Apply · Effective HRM

cards.front: An employee going through a divorce becomes agitated and talks about 'getting even.' Best first step?
choices: Ignore it unless he actually becomes physical
Fire him on the spot with no review
Joke about it to ease the tension
Investigate, refer to the EAP, act promptly
cards.explanation: Take threats seriously: investigate, offer EAP support, and act promptly; failing to act encourages violence.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.16 Apply · Effective HRM

cards.front: Why should supervisors learn to spot warning signs of violence?
choices: To screen out all risky job applicants first
cards.explanation: Most violence stems from unresolved conflict or loss of control; early intervention helps.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.16 Apply · Effective HRM

cards.front: A firm wants a low-cost way for employees to raise conflicts before they boil over. What fits?
cards.explanation: Anonymous channels let people vent conflicts early, before escalation.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.16 Apply · Effective HRM

cards.front: An employee keeps threatening coworkers, but no OSHA standard covers violence. Can OSHA act?
choices: No; violence isn't an OSHA issue
Yes, under the General Duty Clause
cards.explanation: The General Duty Clause can require employers to address threats of violence.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.16 Apply · Legal & Regulatory

cards.front: A company's emergency plan hasn't been reviewed or practiced in years. What should it do?
choices: Review it yearly and run drills
File it with OSHA and wait for feedback
cards.explanation: Review the emergency plan at least yearly and train with drills; plans cover people, resources, and continuity.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.16 Apply · Effective HRM

cards.front: After work, an engineer fully disconnects and relaxes, returning energized. What is this?
cards.explanation: Recovery (relaxation and psychological detachment) restores energy and engagement.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.15 Apply · Effective HRM

cards.front: A worker feels energized and is learning constantly at work. What state is this?
cards.explanation: Thriving combines vitality and learning.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.15 Apply · Effective HRM

cards.front: A hospital cleaner reframes her job around comforting patients. What is this?
cards.explanation: Job crafting reshapes work to make it more meaningful.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.15 Apply · Effective HRM

cards.front: Word bank (engaged, trust, motivation, retention): 'When employees feel safe, they are more likely to be ___.'
cards.explanation: Guide word bank, in order: engaged, trust, motivation, retention.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.19 Apply · Effective HRM

cards.front: Word bank (engaged, trust, motivation, retention): 'A safe environment builds ___, so people share ideas and raise concerns.'
cards.explanation: Safety builds trust, which lets people speak up and collaborate.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.19 Apply · Effective HRM

cards.front: Word bank (engaged, trust, motivation, retention): 'Employees feel more ___ to perform.'
cards.explanation: The guide's sentence: employees feel more motivation to perform.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.19 Apply · Effective HRM

cards.front: Word bank (engaged, trust, motivation, retention): 'Over time, a safe workplace improves ___.'
cards.explanation: People stay where they feel protected and supported, so safety improves retention.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.19 Apply · Effective HRM

cards.front: A plant cuts injuries sharply. Which outcome is most likely to follow?
cards.explanation: Safety boosts morale, engagement, and retention while lowering absences and costs.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.4 Apply · Effective HRM

cards.front: What largely drives the success or failure of adopting a safety culture?
choices: Previous incidents and the accident record
Management and employee norms, beliefs, and assumptions
The perceived trust culture across the whole firm
The cost of running the safety program
cards.explanation: Likely per 12.5 (best guess): management and employee norms, beliefs, and assumptions.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.5 Practice · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 12.5 A Culture of Safety

cards.front: Which agency provides safety information, training, and assistance to employers and workers?
cards.explanation: Likely per 12.7-12.8: OSHA.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.8 Practice · Effective HRM

cards.front: OSHA provides or requires all of the following EXCEPT:
cards.explanation: Likely per 12.7-12.8: free PPE for all workers. Employers must pay for PPE a job requires, but OSHA doesn't hand out PPE or require it for every worker.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.8 Practice · Effective HRM

cards.front: Which is an outcome of employee wellness programs?
cards.explanation: Likely per 12.9: fewer absences.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.9 Practice · Effective HRM

cards.front: An employee is thrilled by a challenging new project. What is she experiencing?
cards.explanation: Likely per 12.11: functional stress.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.11 Practice · Effective HRM

cards.front: An employee is bored because he has too little work. What is he experiencing?
cards.explanation: Likely per 12.11: dysfunctional stress (under-arousal).
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.11 Practice · Effective HRM

cards.front: Which raises workers' comp costs, disability rates, and the risk of a bad reputation?
cards.explanation: Likely per 12.12: bullying.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12.12 Practice · Effective HRM

cards.front: Health and safety topics include disaster preparedness, ergonomics, and ___.
cards.explanation: Likely per 12.11 and 12.15: mental health.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12 Quiz Q1 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 12.11 Stress; 12.15 Creating Sustainable Performance

cards.front: In a strong ___ culture, everyone is responsible for safety every day.
cards.explanation: Likely per 12.5: safety culture.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12 Quiz Q2 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 12.5 A Culture of Safety

cards.front: Which agency inspects on-site or by phone, without advance notice?
cards.explanation: Likely per 12.8: OSHA.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12 Quiz Q3 · Legal & Regulatory

cards.front: Which programs aim to improve the bottom line while building a great workplace?
cards.explanation: Likely per 12.9: wellness programs.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12 Quiz Q4 · Effective HRM

cards.front: Which programs address healthy eating, smoking, weight, physical activity, and stress?
cards.explanation: Likely per 12.9: wellness programs.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12 Quiz Q5 · Effective HRM

cards.front: ___ patterns involve immediate gratification and delayed costs.
cards.explanation: Likely per 12.10: behavioral patterns (present bias).
cards.subtitle: Ch 12 Quiz Q6 · Effective HRM

cards.front: Perceived ___ complicates wellness incentives.
cards.explanation: Likely per 12.10: fairness.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12 Quiz Q7 · Effective HRM

cards.front: Mild ___ releases adrenaline that aids action and memory.
cards.explanation: Likely per 12.11: stress.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12 Quiz Q8 · Effective HRM

cards.front: A(n) ___ level of stress for too long can cause health problems.
cards.explanation: Likely per 12.11: any. The text says prolonged stress of any kind can harm health. Moderate confidence: 'dysfunctional' is tempting, but it's defined by duration already.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12 Quiz Q9 · Effective HRM

cards.front: Conflicting goals, a harsh boss, and boredom are examples of ___ stress.
cards.explanation: Likely per 12.11: dysfunctional stress.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12 Quiz Q10 · Effective HRM

cards.front: Manageable stress that produces positive emotions is ___ stress.
cards.explanation: Likely per 12.11: functional stress.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12 Quiz Q11 · Effective HRM

cards.front: To reduce stress, give employees more ___ over their work patterns.
cards.explanation: Likely per 12.11: control.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12 Quiz Q12 · Effective HRM

cards.front: Heavy workload, unclear responsibilities, and low meaningfulness trigger ___ stress.
cards.explanation: Likely per 12.11: dysfunctional (best fit; the text calls them 'workplace stress triggers'). Moderate confidence.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12 Quiz Q13 · Effective HRM

cards.front: Letting employees ___ reduces stress.
cards.explanation: Likely per 12.11: participation in decisions.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12 Quiz Q14 · Effective HRM

cards.front: Which statement about stress is true?
choices: A lack of stress is not always good
A lack of stress is always good
cards.explanation: Likely per 12.11: a lack of stress isn't always good (boredom is dysfunctional; mild stress helps).
cards.subtitle: Ch 12 Quiz Q15 · Effective HRM

cards.front: Repeated mistreatment through verbal abuse, threats, humiliation, or sabotage is:
cards.explanation: Likely per 12.12: bullying.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12 Quiz Q16 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 12.12 Bullying; 12.19 Summary and Application

cards.front: Anonymous venting channels help prevent workplace ___.
cards.explanation: Likely per 12.16: violence.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12 Quiz Q17 · Effective HRM

cards.front: Any act or threat of violence, harassment, or intimidation at work is ___ violence.
cards.explanation: Likely per 12.16: workplace violence.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12 Quiz Q18 · Effective HRM

cards.front: Most workplace ___ incidents stem from unresolved conflict or a loss of control.
cards.explanation: Likely per 12.16: violence.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12 Quiz Q19 · Effective HRM

cards.front: Done right, ___ programs benefit both employers and employees.
cards.explanation: Likely per 12.9: wellness programs.
cards.subtitle: Ch 12 Quiz Q20 · Effective HRM
